newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Switzerland cuts discount rate to one pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Switzerland cuts discount rate to one pct.

text.p: Switzerland's central bank on Thursday cut its discount rate by half a point to a paltry 1.0 percent, matching a historic low in what analysts described as a clear signal that it wanted the strong Swiss franc to weaken.

Traders pounced on the surprise news to sell the franc against the dollar and mark. Swiss money market rates also fell and prices of short-term debt futures surged, but Swiss shares shrugged off the first discount rate cut since December.

A Swiss National Bank (SNB) statement said the move, which takes effect on Friday, was in line with a recent decline in Swiss money market rates. These rates have fallen below two percent amid a generous flow of liquidity from the central bank.
"By lowering the discount rate, the Swiss National Bank underlines its expectation that the interest rate decline will continue for some time," it said.
"The move is more a reassurance to the market that the interest rate decline since August will not be reversed," SNB spokesman Werner Abegg added.

Many traders were taken by surprise by the timing of the move, although they said the trend was clear given low money market rates, a relatively strong franc and a weak domestic economy that has contracted six quarters in a row.

The franc fell against the dollar and German mark on the news. The dollar was trading around 1.2521 francs by late afternoon, up from 1.2425 before the news. The mark was up around 82.27 Swiss centimes per mark from about 81.90.

Analysts suggested the SNB was moving away from its strict traditional adherence to money supply targets and instead turning its focus to the franc, whose strength has hamstrung the Swiss economy by crimping crucial exports.

"For us this is a clear signal that they are conducting currency exchange rate policy and that money supply growth plays no role at all any more," said Rainer Marian at CS Economic Research in Zurich.
He said foreign exchange speculators could now safely assume that 82.5 Swiss centimes per mark no longer had to be the perceived upper limit for the German currency, as in the past.

Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust in London, said the SNB sought to make the franc less attractive to investors wary about the stability of Europe's single currency, to arrive in 1999 as part of economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The Swiss are worried about the impact of a fudged EMU on the Swiss franc. They're trying to pre-empt any upward pressure on the franc by cutting rates," he said.

If so, the SNB has precious little room to cut rates should the flow of such funds turn into a flood. But Peter Buomberger, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) chief economist, said the SNB could do little in any event to hold back the tide if it came.
"In the case of massive speculative flows, the only thing they could do is peg the franc" to the single currency, he said, even though SNB officials say this would be the absolute last resort.

The discount rate, which plays a relatively limited role in Swiss markets but packs a symbolic punch, was last cut to a record low one percent in February 1978, It stayed there until it returned to 2.0 percent in November 1979.
UBS analyst Manfred Gutmann said Thursday's cut was not unexpected because short-term market rates had fallen below the discount rate, warranting a move to restore the status quo.
Nevertheless, the move sent a strong signal that the SNB would keep liquidity high, he added.
"This is a signal that they will continue their relatively strong supply of money...The signal is they want the Swiss franc exchange rate lower," Gutmann said.

Industry groups hailed the step as a move to spur growth, but Guttman said he expected no big boost to the real economy. UBS stuck to its forecast that the economy would grow 0.8 percent in 1997 after contracting 0.6 percent this year.
